run.name: Senate 450K 2601
run.description: GerryChain ReCom MCMC ensemble — senate redistricting, 450,005 draws across 6 elections.

dem_seats.label: Seat–Vote Proportionality
dem_seats.headline: Does the seat count reflect how people actually voted?
dem_seats.description: In a fair map, the share of seats each party wins should reflect its share of statewide votes. This metric counts districts projected to lean Democratic based on each plan's vote patterns — not as a partisan goal, but as a measuring stick for proportionality. The histogram shows how many Democratic-leaning seats thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. If the enacted map falls far from this range, lines were likely drawn to systematically over- or under-represent one party.
dem_seats.takeaway: The enacted map produces 23 Democratic-leaning seats — at the 41th percentile, within the typical range for neutral maps (median: 24, range: 22–26). No significant seat-count advantage detected for either party.

formula_info.detail: dem_2pv_d = Σ dem_votes_vtd / Σ (dem_votes_vtd + rep_votes_vtd) for all VTDs in district d
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 five-election average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov+Senate avg, 2024 Pres)

efficiency_gap.label: Wasted Votes Balance
efficiency_gap.headline: Are both parties' votes equally effective at winning representation?
efficiency_gap.description: Every election produces 'wasted' votes — votes cast in losing districts (all wasted) and surplus votes beyond what was needed to win (also wasted). A fair map wastes votes at roughly equal rates for both parties. The Efficiency Gap measures the difference: a positive value means one party's votes are being wasted at a higher rate than the other's — a sign that district lines are concentrating or dispersing that party's voters artificially. Developed by Stephanopoulos & McGhee; cited in federal gerrymandering litigation.
efficiency_gap.takeaway: The enacted map's efficiency gap (0.078) is above the neutral median (0.055), at the 83th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps. Democratic votes are wasted at a higher rate, giving Republicans a structural advantage in translating votes to seats.

formula_info.formula: (Σ wasted_dem − Σ wasted_rep) / Σ total_votes  across all districts
formula_info.detail: wasted_dem = excess Dem votes beyond 50%+1 in Dem wins + all Dem votes in Dem losses; symmetric for Rep

mean_median.label: Vote Distribution Symmetry
mean_median.headline: Does each party need the same number of votes to win a district?
mean_median.description: The Mean-Median difference reveals whether one party's votes are systematically spread more efficiently across districts than the other's. When one party wins many districts by modest margins while the other piles up large majorities in fewer districts, the map gives the first party a structural seat advantage — even when both parties receive equal votes statewide. A value near zero means both parties convert votes to seats at roughly the same rate. A large deviation in either direction is a signal of asymmetric voter distribution — often a hallmark of gerrymandering.
mean_median.takeaway: The mean–median difference (0.090) is above the neutral median (0.041), at the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic voters are disproportionately concentrated in fewer districts, giving Republicans a more efficient geographic spread of support.

formula_info.detail: Positive → Dem votes distributed less efficiently across districts (Republican structural advantage). Negative → reverse.

comp_seats_7pt.label: Electoral Competitiveness (7-pt)
comp_seats_7pt.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats_7pt.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats_7pt.takeaway: The enacted map has zero competitive districts within the 5pp threshold. At the 0th percentile, this is an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Every district has a predetermined partisan lean — voters have no meaningful choice in any race.

formula_info.detail: A district is competitive if the two-party Democratic share falls within ±competitive_margin of 50%

dem_safe_seats.label: Safe Democratic Seats
dem_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Democratic — beyond the competitive margin?
dem_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Democratic two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Democratic and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Republican seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Democratic voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
dem_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 23.000. Neutral median: 21.000 (range: 19.000–23.000). At the 98th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps.

formula_info.detail: Democratic-leaning districts outside the competitive zone — margin exceeds threshold on the Democratic side

comp_seats_10pt.label: Electoral Competitiveness (10-pt)
comp_seats_10pt.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats_10pt.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats_10pt.takeaway: The enacted map has just 2 competitive district(s) — fewer than 100% of neutral maps. Most voters live in districts where outcomes are predetermined.

dem_safe_seats.label: Safe Democratic Seats
dem_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Democratic — beyond the competitive margin?
dem_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Democratic two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Democratic and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Republican seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Democratic voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
dem_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 23.000. Neutral median: 23.000 (range: 21.000–25.000). At the 69th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps.

dem_seats.label: Seat–Vote Proportionality
dem_seats.headline: Does the seat count reflect how people actually voted?
dem_seats.description: In a fair map, the share of seats each party wins should reflect its share of statewide votes. This metric counts districts projected to lean Democratic based on each plan's vote patterns — not as a partisan goal, but as a measuring stick for proportionality. The histogram shows how many Democratic-leaning seats thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. If the enacted map falls far from this range, lines were likely drawn to systematically over- or under-represent one party.
dem_seats.takeaway: The enacted map produces 23 Democratic-leaning seats — at the 12th percentile, below the neutral median of 25 (range: 23–27). This is within the normal range for neutral maps, suggesting a structural seat advantage for Republicans.

formula_info.detail: dem_2pv_d = Σ dem_votes_vtd / Σ (dem_votes_vtd + rep_votes_vtd) for all VTDs in district d
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 five-election average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov+Senate avg, 2024 Pres)

efficiency_gap.label: Wasted Votes Balance
efficiency_gap.headline: Are both parties' votes equally effective at winning representation?
efficiency_gap.description: Every election produces 'wasted' votes — votes cast in losing districts (all wasted) and surplus votes beyond what was needed to win (also wasted). A fair map wastes votes at roughly equal rates for both parties. The Efficiency Gap measures the difference: a positive value means one party's votes are being wasted at a higher rate than the other's — a sign that district lines are concentrating or dispersing that party's voters artificially. Developed by Stephanopoulos & McGhee; cited in federal gerrymandering litigation.
efficiency_gap.takeaway: The enacted map's efficiency gap (0.103) is above the neutral median (0.052), at the 98th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic votes are wasted at a higher rate, giving Republicans a structural advantage in translating votes to seats.

formula_info.formula: (Σ wasted_dem − Σ wasted_rep) / Σ total_votes  across all districts
formula_info.detail: wasted_dem = excess Dem votes beyond 50%+1 in Dem wins + all Dem votes in Dem losses; symmetric for Rep

mean_median.label: Vote Distribution Symmetry
mean_median.headline: Does each party need the same number of votes to win a district?
mean_median.description: The Mean-Median difference reveals whether one party's votes are systematically spread more efficiently across districts than the other's. When one party wins many districts by modest margins while the other piles up large majorities in fewer districts, the map gives the first party a structural seat advantage — even when both parties receive equal votes statewide. A value near zero means both parties convert votes to seats at roughly the same rate. A large deviation in either direction is a signal of asymmetric voter distribution — often a hallmark of gerrymandering.
mean_median.takeaway: The mean–median difference (0.069) is above the neutral median (0.031), at the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic voters are disproportionately concentrated in fewer districts, giving Republicans a more efficient geographic spread of support.

formula_info.detail: Positive → Dem votes distributed less efficiently across districts (Republican structural advantage). Negative → reverse.

maj_black.label: Black Community Representation
maj_black.headline: Do Black voters have the opportunity to elect representatives of their choice?
maj_black.description: This counts districts where Black Voting Age Population (BVAP) makes up at least 20% of total Voting Age Population — the influence/coalition threshold. Under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, mapmakers must not draw lines that dilute minority communities' ability to elect their preferred candidates. The histogram shows how many influence-level Black districts thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. Standard Princeton symmetric grading is used: both unusually low and unusually high counts are flagged relative to the neutral ensemble. Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (not ACS estimates).
maj_black.takeaway: The enacted map has 34 majority-Black district(s) — fewer than 94% of neutral maps (neutral range: 34–39). This is significantly below what geography alone would suggest, raising potential Voting Rights Act concerns.

formula_info.detail: Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (Table P4, P0040006 NH Black alone / P0040001 Total VAP). Headcounts — not ACS estimates.

min_coal.label: Minority Coalition Representation
min_coal.headline: Do communities of color collectively hold electoral influence?
min_coal.description: This counts districts where non-white Voting Age Population makes up at least 20% of total VAP — communities of color collectively hold influence even when no single racial group holds a majority. Standard Princeton symmetric grading is used: both unusually low and unusually high counts relative to the neutral ensemble are flagged. Uses 2020 Census PL 94-171 headcounts (not ACS estimates).
min_coal.takeaway: The enacted map has 53 minority-coalition district(s), within the typical range for neutral maps (52–54).

formula_info.detail: Combined non-white VAP share (1 − NH White fraction). A minority-coalition district includes multiple racial groups, none individually a majority.

maj_white.label: Majority-White Districts
maj_white.headline: How many districts have a white-citizen majority of eligible voters?
maj_white.description: Counts districts where non-Hispanic white citizens make up more than 20% of the Citizen Voting Age Population. Shown alongside minority representation metrics to complete the full demographic picture of how the map distributes political power across racial groups. The Princeton ensemble test grades statistical distance from neutral redistricting outcomes symmetrically — unusually high or low counts compared to neutral maps both indicate the map departs from geography-driven redistricting.
maj_white.takeaway: The enacted map has 54 majority-white districts — more than 100% of neutral maps (typical range: 50–53). This is statistically unusual and may indicate minority vote dilution or cracking of diverse communities.

formula_info.detail: Districts where non-Hispanic white citizens are a majority of eligible voters (2020 Census P0040005). Shown alongside minority metrics to complete the demographic picture.

min_influence.label: Minority Influence Districts
min_influence.headline: How many districts give communities of color meaningful electoral influence without a majority?
min_influence.description: Counts districts where communities of color collectively hold between the FDGA influence floor (37%) and the majority threshold (50%) of the Citizen Voting Age Population. These districts are below the threshold for direct Section 2 Voting Rights Act protection but above the level at which minority voters can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes and hold candidates accountable. More influence districts indicates broader minority electoral participation. Both thresholds are configurable.
min_influence.takeaway: The enacted map has 11 minority influence district(s) — fewer than 100% of neutral maps (typical range: 14–21). Communities of color have fewer districts where they can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes than neutral redistricting would typically produce.

formula_info.detail: Districts where communities of color have meaningful electoral influence but do not constitute a majority. Below the majority threshold for direct VRA Section 2 protection, but above the FDGA influence floor where minority voters can meaningfully affect outcomes.

muni_splits.label: Split Cities & Municipalities
muni_splits.headline: How many cities and towns are divided across different districts?
muni_splits.description: Counts incorporated municipalities (cities, towns) whose territory is split across two or more congressional districts. Urban cracking — dividing a city among multiple districts — dilutes its collective political voice and reduces the ability of city residents to elect a single representative who understands local concerns. Fewer splits means more communities are kept intact. The neutral ensemble shows how many splits geography-driven redistricting would typically produce; the enacted map is compared against this baseline.
muni_splits.takeaway: The enacted map splits just 40 cities and municipalities — fewer than 98% of neutral maps (typical range: 42–57). Urban communities are exceptionally well preserved compared to what neutral redistricting would produce.

formula_info.formula: count(municipalities m : ∃ VTDs v1, v2 ∈ m assigned to different districts)
formula_info.detail: An incorporated municipality (city, town) is 'split' when at least two of its VTDs are assigned to different districts. Urban cracking indicator.
